slides.headline: Three hearts and blue blood.
slides.sub: And two-thirds of its neurons live in its arms. Meet Octopus cyanea

slides.headline: Two of its hearts work only for the gills
slides.body: Two branchial hearts push blood through the gills to pick up oxygen. The third, the systemic heart, sends it on to the organs and muscles.

slides.headline: Its main heart stops when it swims
slides.body: Jetting through open water halts the systemic heart. That is why octopuses usually crawl instead: swimming exhausts them.

slides.headline: Its blood is blue
slides.body: Oxygen rides on hemocyanin, a copper-based protein, instead of the iron-based hemoglobin in our blood. The copper makes the blood look blue.

slides.label: of its ~500 million neurons sit in its arms
slides.body: The central brain acts more like a coordinator. Much of the sensing and movement control happens out in the arms themselves.

slides.headline: A rare daytime hunter
slides.body: Unlike most octopuses, it forages by day, then blocks its den with rocks at night. It lives only about 12–15 months.

slides.headline: Eight arms. Three hearts. One save.
slides.body: Keep it for your next trivia night. New species, fully sourced, every week.
sources: Hochner, B. (2012) An embodied view of octopus neurobiology. Current Biology 22:R887–R892
Smithsonian Magazine (2024): Ten Wild Facts About Octopuses

caption:
The big blue octopus (Octopus cyanea) runs on three hearts and copper-based blue blood, with most of its neurons in its arms.

Also called the day octopus, it lives on coral reefs from Hawaii to the Red Sea at depths of about 1 to 100 m. Its name means dark blue, after the dark blue rings on its skin. Every photo here was taken on a reef at Nosy Tanikely, Madagascar.

Swipe through the anatomy. Sources on the last slide.
